An Albanese government minister has doubled down on his claims Liberal icon Sir Robert Menzies was a “Nazi appeaser,” saying he would “absolutely not” withdraw his comments after being asked to apologise for the incident.

Fronting media on Friday, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said he would “absolutely not” apologise for relaying “a historical fact” during a speech he made at the National Press Club this week.

“Labor is the party of national security … We’re proud of our record, and I’m not going to take a step back,” Mr Conroy told Nine’s Today.

When asked if he had been engaging in needless culture war back-and-forth, Mr Conroy accused the Liberals of blowing the comments up, saying they are “a party that has no relevance and they’re desperately trying for it right now.”

“They’re the ones who interrupted parliament with this hysterical stunt,” Mr Conroy said.

“In the end, you can’t argue with history in the history.”

Liberal frontbencher Dan Tehan called the “Nazi appeaser” comment an “utter, utter disgrace” as parliamentarians filed out of the House of Representatives shortly after parliamentary question time on Thursday.

Mr Tehan attempted to have Mr Conroy “sanctioned” over his comments only hours earlier, though a suspension of standing orders to move the motion was swiftly quashed by Labor’s massive majority.

Mr Tehan claimed another MP went on to brand Sir Robert – the founder of the Liberal Party and Australia’s longest-serving prime minister – a “coward” and called for whoever made the statement to withdraw it.

During Mr Conroy’s National Press Club address earlier in the day, he declared his “great hero” was Labor wartime prime minister John Curtin.

“I consume his biographies. I’m very interested in disclosing what really happened before World War II and during World War II, where it was a choice between John Curtin and Nazi-appeaser Robert Gordon Menzies,” he said.

“This is really important stuff that the Left needs to embrace more fully.”

The Australian reported that while Mr Tehan and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke argued over the motion, Mr Conroy stood ready to table a letter from Sir Robert to Australia’s high commissioner in London eight days after committing Australia to war supporting negotiations with German leader Adolf Hitler.

The September 11, 1939 letter was released in 2001.

In it, he urged for talks with Hitler and said “nobody really gives a damn about Poland”.

He said the war would not be sustained “by the cry of ‘Down with the Nazi government’ for it is really quite indefensible for us to be dictating to the German people what sort of Government they shall have”.

“The cry then must be, in effect, `Law and order and an end of terrorism in Europe’,” it said.

“I don’t underestimate this cry, because I believe it is true and a good one.”

Sir Robert served twice as prime minister between 1939-1941, as war got under way in Europe, and again as the dust settled between 1949 and 1966.

Menzies Research Centre executive director David Hughes said it was unfair to “reduce complex history to partisan attacks”.

“Apply that method to (former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill) and even the man most associated with defeating Hitler can be distorted by selective quotes,” he said.

“Serious history looks at the whole record, not convenient fragments.”

He noted that Sir Robert was the prime minister who broke the news to Australians that the country was at war with Nazi Germany.

“In that address he described Hitler’s ambition as the subjugation of European nations by force,” Mr Hughes said.

He said Mr Conroy “is right to admire John Curtin”, calling Mr Curtin “a great wartime prime minister”.

“But Curtin’s own pre-war record was more complicated than Labor mythology allows,” he said.

“He opposed Menzies’ compulsory training scheme and, like many leaders of the time, sought to avoid conflict with Japan for as long as possible.

“In 1941 he was still engaging privately with Japan’s minister to Australia, Tatsuo Kawai.

“None of that diminishes Curtin’s greatness. He rose to the moment history demanded. Pat Conroy needs to do the same.”

Labor, including Mr Conroy and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, have repeatedly called for a “progressive patriotism” in recent months amid a surge in support for One Nation and renewed security challenges.

Originally published as Minister doubles down on comments calling ex-PM Robert Menzies a ‘Nazi appeaser’
